content: When mothers become ill or pass away, their children often suffer due to the loss of usual care. HIV-infected children, being immunocompromised, experience high mortality rates even without the added burden of severe acute malnutrition. However, when these children also suffer from severe acute malnutrition, their risk of death during nutritional rehabilitation therapy is nearly three times higher compared to HIV-negative children. These children are also more prone to persistent diarrhea and opportunistic infections such as tuberculosis, cryptosporidiosis, disseminated candidiasis, and cryptococcosis. Despite these well-documented clinical patterns, there has been limited research on the management of HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) has proven effective in significantly reducing opportunistic infections and improving survival rates in both HIV-infected adults and children, offering hope for better outcomes. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends initiating ART for all infants under 24 months of age, regardless of clinical condition, and for children older than 24 months if they meet specific criteria, such as unexplained malnutrition. WHO also advises routine HIV screening for children showing clinical signs of infection or malnutrition to assess their eligibility for ART. In settings with high HIV prevalence (greater than 1%), children with malnutrition should be tested for HIV to determine their status and need for ART. Simplified dosing schedules for ART based on weight bands are provided by WHO. However, individuals and families affected by HIV are often targeted by commercial products claiming to offer specific benefits, many of which lack evidence of efficacy. It is crucial to identify interventions that provide real clinical benefits to HIV-infected individuals. Key issues in the care of HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition include determining the optimal timing and dosing of ART, appropriate feeding regimens, and the value of vitamin A supplementation. A systematic review found no randomized controlled trials directly addressing these questions in this population. Observational studies suggest that low weight-for-age is associated with increased mortality and complications such as immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome. Starting ART within 21 days of admission for therapeutic feeding has shown improved recovery compared to delayed initiation. However, there is no data on the outcomes of different ART regimens or therapeutic feeding approaches in this group. Vitamin A supplementation has been shown to improve growth and reduce mortality in HIV-infected children without severe malnutrition, but its specific effects in those with severe acute malnutrition remain untested. Similarly, while zinc supplementation is safe in HIV-infected children without severe malnutrition, its role in managing diarrhea in this population is unclear. Given the lack of adverse effects, zinc should not be excluded from routine management. The WHO emphasizes that all HIV-exposed infants and children, including those with severe acute malnutrition, should be tested for HIV. ART should be initiated as soon as possible after stabilizing metabolic complications and sepsis, indicated by the return of appetite and resolution of severe edema. HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition should receive the same ART regimens and doses as those without malnutrition. Close monitoring during the first 6–8 weeks of ART initiation is essential to detect early complications and infections. Management of severe acute malnutrition in HIV-infected children should follow the same therapeutic feeding approaches as for uninfected children. High-dose vitamin A and zinc should be provided unless the child is already receiving fortified therapeutic foods. Persistent diarrhea in these children should prompt investigations for carbohydrate intolerance and infectious causes, which may require tailored management. For infants under six months of age, severe acute malnutrition is increasingly recognized, often linked to suboptimal breastfeeding practices. Exclusive breastfeeding is critical for optimal nutrition and infection protection, yet global rates remain low. Mortality is higher in young infants with severe acute malnutrition compared to older children, but the extent of avoidable mortality is unclear. Management in this age group focuses on re-establishing exclusive breastfeeding, with formula feeding or early complementary foods used when breastfeeding is not possible. However, physiological differences in young infants necessitate modified management approaches. Admission and discharge criteria for infants under six months with severe acute malnutrition are not well-defined. Limited evidence exists on therapeutic feeding protocols for this age group, and no studies have examined feeding approaches during the transition and rehabilitation phases. Supplemental sucking techniques have been used successfully in some cases, but practices such as transitioning to rehabilitation phases remain underexplored. The guideline development group highlighted the need for further research on early ART initiation, optimal dosing, and therapeutic feeding approaches for HIV-infected children with severe acute malnutrition. They also emphasized the importance of programmatic guidance for healthcare workers managing these vulnerable populations.
